summary: Specifies a data model for synchronising contact data with a server using the JSON Meta Application Protocol (JMAP).

plainLanguage.summary: Your phone and laptop should show the same contacts. This explains how they keep one address book in sync over JMAP.

subtitle: How a JMAP client and server keep address books and contact cards in sync.

tldr.problem: People keep contacts on several devices and want them to match everywhere, but the core JMAP protocol only describes generic synchronisation, not what a contact is.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9610 defines two JMAP data types: AddressBook, a named collection, and ContactCard, a JSContact card with two extra properties. Both reuse the standard JMAP get, changes, query, set and copy methods.
tldr.outcome: Clients can fetch, search, create, share and organise contacts with the same request style they use for other JMAP data. It is a Proposed Standard with no replacement.

today: RFC 9610 is a Proposed Standard published in December 2024, and the metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on JMAP (RFC 8620), JSContact (RFC 9553) and JMAP Sharing (RFC 9670).

sections.title: What JMAP Contacts Adds
sections.content:
The JSON Meta Application Protocol (JMAP), defined in RFC 8620, is a generic protocol for synchronising data such as mail, calendars or contacts between a client and a server. RFC 9610 adds the contacts part: a data model for synchronising contacts over JMAP.

An account that supports contacts holds zero or more AddressBook objects. Each AddressBook is a named collection of zero or more ContactCard objects. A ContactCard represents a person, company, entity or a group of such entities, and it is a JSContact Card as defined in RFC 9553. Each card belongs to one or more address books.

Servers that also support JMAP Sharing (RFC 9670) let users see and configure sharing of contact data. Sharing permissions are managed per AddressBook.
sections.plainLanguage: An address book is like a labelled box, and each contact card is a card inside it. One card can sit in more than one box.

sections.title: The Contacts Capability
sections.content:
A server announces support with the capability URI urn:ietf:params:jmap:contacts. In the JMAP Session object's capabilities property its value is an empty object. In an account's accountCapabilities it is an object that MUST carry two pieces of information.

  • maxAddressBooksPerCard: the most AddressBooks one ContactCard can be in. It MUST be an integer of at least 1, or null for no limit.
  • mayCreateAddressBook: the user may create an AddressBook in this account if, and only if, this is true.
sections.plainLanguage: Before using contacts, the app asks the server what it allows, like checking the rules of a library before borrowing books.

sections.title: AddressBooks and Their Rights
sections.content:
An AddressBook has these main properties: a server-set id, a name, an optional description, a sortOrder, isDefault, isSubscribed, shareWith and myRights.

The name MUST NOT be empty and MUST NOT be greater than 255 octets when encoded as UTF-8. sortOrder lets every device list address books in the same order; a lower number is shown first, and ties are sorted alphabetically by name. isDefault SHOULD be true for exactly one AddressBook in an account and MUST NOT be true for more than one. Clients use the default when they have no other basis to choose, for example when the user creates a new card.

isSubscribed says whether the user wants to see the book. It SHOULD default to false for books in shared accounts and true for books the user creates. An unsubscribed book and its contents SHOULD be shown only when the user asks.

Access is described by an AddressBookRights object with four booleans: mayRead, mayWrite, mayShare and mayDelete. myRights shows the user's own rights, and shareWith maps Principal ids to the rights given to others. It is null when the book is not shared or the server does not support RFC 9670.
sections.plainLanguage: Each box has a name, a place in the list, and rules about who may look inside, change things, share it or throw it away.

sections.title: Methods for AddressBooks
sections.content:
AddressBook uses the standard JMAP /get, /changes and /set methods from RFC 8620. For AddressBook/get, the ids argument may be null to fetch everything at once.

AddressBook/set adds two request arguments:

  • onDestroyRemoveContents (default false): if false, destroying an AddressBook that still holds a card is rejected with an addressBookHasContents SetError. If true, the cards are removed from it, and any card in no other book is destroyed.
  • onSuccessSetIsDefault: if all other changes succeed, the server tries to make this book the default. If the id is not found or policy forbids it, the request is ignored without an error.

Changing shareWith needs the mayShare right, and a user cannot give a Principal a right the user does not have; attempts MUST be rejected with a forbidden SetError. A server MAY also refuse a subscription change with forbidden.
sections.plainLanguage: If you try to throw away a box with cards still in it, the server says no, unless you said up front that the cards should go too.

sections.title: ContactCards, Groups and Photos
sections.content:
A ContactCard is a JSContact Card with two added properties. id is server-set and may differ from the card's uid, but there MUST NOT be two cards with the same uid in one account. addressBookIds is an object whose keys are AddressBook ids and whose values MUST be true; a card MUST belong to at least one book until it is destroyed.

For any Media object, a new blobId property is defined. When returning cards, any Media whose URI uses the data: scheme SHOULD return a blobId and omit the uri, so clients load a large image only when needed and avoid Base64 overhead. The mediaType MUST also be set. To set a new photo, the client first uploads the file with the JMAP upload mechanism, and the server MUST reject a file that is not a recognised image type.

A card whose kind is group represents a group of contacts. Its members property lists the uids of the members, which clients resolve across every account that supports the contacts capability. A uid that cannot be found SHOULD be ignored but preserved, so a member who disappears after losing access to a shared book reappears when access returns.
sections.plainLanguage: A contact card is a card with a name and details. A photo is kept in a separate drawer and the card just points to it, so the card stays light.

sections.title: Searching and Sorting Cards
sections.content:
ContactCard uses the standard /get, /changes, /query, /queryChanges, /set and /copy methods. The new content is mostly in /query.

A FilterCondition can test inAddressBook, uid, hasMember, kind, the created and updated dates (createdBefore, createdAfter, updatedBefore, updatedAfter), a free text search, and fields such as name, name/given, name/surname, nickname, organization, email, phone, onlineService, address and note. An empty condition always matches, and when several properties are given all of them must match.

The exact matching of strings is deliberately left to the server. Text SHOULD be matched case-insensitively, quoted text SHOULD be a phrase search, unquoted words separated by whitespace MUST all be present, and tokens MAY be matched by stemming.

Servers MUST support sorting by created and updated, and SHOULD support name/given, name/surname and name/surname2.
sections.plainLanguage: You can ask the server to find cards by name, email or phone, and to list them by date. It is a bit like asking a librarian to look something up.

sections.title: A Worked Exchange
sections.content:
The RFC shows a client that has authenticated and fetched the Session object, found one account with the contacts capability (id a0x9), and wants everything. It sends one request containing AddressBook/get and ContactCard/get. The server answers with two address books, Personal (the default) and Autosaved, and one card for Joe Bloggs with an email address.

A second example changes the default book. The client sends AddressBook/set with only onSuccessSetIsDefault set to the id of Autosaved. The server allows it and reports both books as updated: isDefault becomes true on one and false on the other, with the state moving from ~4144 to ~4148.
sections.plainLanguage: The app asks for all the boxes and cards in one go, and later asks to move the star that marks the favourite box.

sections.title: Privacy, Unicode and Security
sections.content:
All security considerations of JMAP apply. The RFC adds that contacts are almost entirely private, personally identifiable information and reflect users' social connections, so privacy leaks can have real-world consequences. Servers MUST enforce the access control lists set on address books so only authorised data is shared.

The Internationalisation Considerations warn that unrestricted Unicode can cause inconsistent rendering and misreading. A server MAY restrict the characters allowed in free String fields, for which the FreeformClass in RFC 8264 might be a starting point. For forbidden code points the server can strip or replace them with U+FFFD, returning any changed properties in the /set response, or it MAY reject the change with an invalidProperties SetError.
sections.plainLanguage: Contacts are private, like a diary of who you know, so the server must only show them to people who are allowed to see them.
